Integrating Water-Quality Analysis in Ecuador's National Household Surveys A study by Moreno et al. highlighted the integration of water-quality analysis into Ecuador's national household surveys, focusing on water and sanitation sector learnings. This approach aimed to address gaps in drinking water regulatory frameworks and mechanisms, particularly in rural areas. For instance, in Cabo Verde, the proportion of the rural population accessing at least basic water supply services increased from 72% in 2012 to 83% in 2022, attributed to sector reforms and the establishment of two autonomous regulatory agencies. These agencies developed comprehensive regulatory mechanisms, including standards, incentives, sanctions, and performance reporting, which were previously lacking when regulatory responsibilities were held within ministries. 2. Addressing Institutional Fragmentation in Israel's Water Sector The Israeli Water Authority, established in 2007, consolidated planning, development, management, and regulation of the water sector, including small drinking-water suppliers. This reform addressed institutional fragmentation by creating a formalized decision-making body, the Israeli Water Authority Council, which includes representatives from various ministries and public representatives. This council has improved sector planning and policy development, making them more cohesive and effective. 3. Financing Rural Drinking-Water Services in Uganda Uganda's Ministry of Water and Environment has transformed six regional water and sanitation support organizations into utilities focused on small towns and rural growth centers. These utilities, known as umbrellas, have significantly improved access, service reliability, and water quality. For example, the proportion of the rural population using uncontaminated water supplies increased from 34% in 2015 to 56% in 2022. Sustainable financing sources, including user fees, subsidies, and revenue from other activities, have been critical to these improvements. 4. Capacity Development for Small Water Supply Operators in the United States In the U.S., over 97% of public water systems are small supplies serving fewer than 10,000 people. The 1996 Safe Drinking Water Act Amendments require states to develop capacity-building programs to assist these systems in building technical, managerial, and financial capacities. Operator certification programs vary by state, with requirements tailored to the size and complexity of facilities. For example, in Hawaii, operators must meet specific educational and work experience requirements based on facility classification. 5. Adapting Monitoring Frameworks for Rural Water Supplies in Peru Peru has implemented reforms to improve the monitoring and regulation of rural water services, which are predominantly managed by community-based organizations. The 2016 Framework Law on Sanitation Services Management introduced a revised monitoring and regulatory mandate for rural areas, emphasizing efficiency and sustainability. The National Superintendence of Sanitation Services has adapted its monitoring approach to rural conditions, focusing on fewer parameters and lower reporting frequency compared to urban areas. 6. Strategic Planning for Rural Water Services in Zambia Zambia has reformed its rural water supply sector by mandating 11 commercial utilities to provide safe and reliable services. The National Water Supply and Sanitation Council developed a framework in 2018 to operationalize these reforms, including an implementation plan, monitoring processes, and budget requirements. 7. Professionalizing Community-Based Water Management in Uganda Uganda's Ministry of Water and Environment has introduced a professionalized model of community-based management, known as Community-Based Management Plus. This model delegates key maintenance and repair functions to area service providers, such as private operators, through performance contracts. For example, Whave Solutions, an area service provider, reports functionality rates of 94–97% and repairs completed within one day for 90% of cases, significantly improving water supply performance. 8. Expanding Utility Management of Rural Water Services in Africa and Asia Utility-managed rural water services are becoming more common in lowand middle-income countries. Examples include Rwanda's Byumba Local Public-Private Partnership Model, Senegal's Hydraulic Works Operating Company, and Uganda's umbrella water authorities. These utilities generally outperform traditional community-managed systems in terms of supply hours, water quality, and operational cost coverage. 9. Engaging Small Water Suppliers in Regulation Development in New Zealand New Zealand's Water Services Act 2021 expanded the scope of regulated water supplies to include very small community supplies serving up to 25 people. Taumata Arowai, the national drinking-water regulator, engaged extensively with small water suppliers to address resistance to regulation. This included consultations and revisions to standards and rules, reducing the scope of required activities while ensuring public health protection. 10. Indigenous-Owned Water Supplier Contributions to Regulation in Canada In Canada, First Nations communities on reserves lack legally enforceable drinking-water protections. The Atlantic First Nations Water Authority, established in 2018 as the first Indigenous-owned water utility, has been a leading proponent of regulations and standards for drinking-water services. The Government of Canada is developing new legislation in consultation with First Nations to establish national standards for drinking water and wastewater on First Nations lands. These case studies illustrate diverse approaches to improving water supply management, regulation, and service delivery across different regions and contexts.
